label: Divrei HaYamim Bet (2 Chronicles) — Part 2 — Chapters 19–36
summary_plain: Divrei HaYamim Bet chapters 19 through 36 trace the southern kingdom from Yehoshafat through the destruction of Yerushalayim. Yehoshafat establishes judges and says: Consider what you do — for you judge not for man but for YHWH. Chizkiyahu (Hezekiah) cleanse the temple, restores Pesach, and trusts YHWH against Sennacherib of Ashur. Yoshiyahu (Josiah) finds the Torah scroll in the temple and tears his garments — he renews the covenant and celebrates the greatest Pesach since Shemu'el. But the decline continues. Yerushalayim falls to Nevukhadnetzar. The temple is burned. The people are exiled to Babylon. The final verse is Koresh's decree: let the exiles go up.
summary_scholarly: The ACR reads from DSS fragments and the Orit Ge'ez. The Chronicler's account of the southern kingdom emphasizes a cycle: reform, apostasy, judgment. Chizkiyahu (chapters 29-32) and Yoshiyahu (chapters 34-35) represent the high points — both kings cleanse the temple, restore Torah observance, and celebrate Pesach. Yoshiyahu's discovery of the Torah scroll (34:14-21) is critical: the Torah was lost within the temple itself. The book of the covenant had to be rediscovered. This is the Great Eraser pattern within the covenant community's own history — the text can be lost even when the institution that houses it still stands. The Chronicler's final verse (36:23) is Koresh's decree — the same decree that opens Ezra. The destruction is not the final word. The exile is not permanent. YHWH moves a Persian king to restore what Babylon destroyed.

key_terms.definition: Khizkiyahu invites all Yisra'el and Yehudah to a great Passover in Yerushalayim — the greatest celebration since the days of Shlomo, drawing even from the northern tribes
Yoshiyahu begins seeking YHWH at age sixteen, tears down the high places and altars of Ba'al, and purges idolatry throughout Yehudah and even into the northern territories
The high priest Khilqiyahu finds the Book of Torah in the Temple while it is being repaired — Yoshiyahu tears his clothes in distress when it is read to him
The Passover Yoshiyahu celebrates is declared the greatest since the days of Shemu'el the prophet — Divrei HaYamim rates it higher than Khizkiyahu's
Yoshiyahu goes out to fight Pharaoh Nekho at Megiddo against the word of YHWH — he is fatally wounded and dies in Yerushalayim; all Yehudah and Yerushalayim mourn for him
The final chapter narrates the last four kings (Yehoakhaz, Yehoyaqim, Yehoyakhin, Tzidkiyahu), Nebukhadnetzar's invasions, the destruction of the Temple, and the exile to Babylon
YHWH's compassion on his people before the destruction: he sent his messengers again and again, but the people mocked the messengers and despised his words until there was no remedy
The final verses of Divrei HaYamim are identical to the opening of Ezra — Cyrus king of Persia declares YHWH has given him all the kingdoms and commands rebuilding the Temple in Yerushalayim
The exile fulfills the word of YHWH through Yirmeyahu — the land enjoys its Shabbat rests for 70 years, until the land had made up its full Shabbat debt
The last king of Yehudah — installed by Nebukhadnetzar; did evil; refused to humble himself before YHWH or Yirmeyahu the prophet; rebelled against Babylon, bringing the final destruction

faq.question: What makes Khizkiyahu's Passover unusual?
faq.answer: He invites all of Yisra'el — including the northern tribes — to come to Yerushalayim, though many in the north mocked his messengers. Those who came celebrated for two weeks instead of one, and the joy was compared to Shlomo's day.

faq.question: What is Yoshiyahu's significance in Divrei HaYamim?
faq.answer: He is the last great covenant-reform king of Yehudah. He began seeking YHWH as a teenager before the Torah was even found, then undertook sweeping covenant renewal when the Book of Torah was discovered in the Temple.

faq.question: What happened when the Book of Torah was found in the Temple?
faq.answer: Yoshiyahu tore his clothes in grief when it was read — recognizing how far Yehudah had strayed from its commands. He sent to the prophetess Khuldah, who confirmed the promised judgment but also that YHWH would spare Yoshiyahu from seeing the disaster.

faq.question: Why is Yoshiyahu's Passover rated greater than Khizkiyahu's in Divrei HaYamim?
faq.answer: Divrei HaYamim states that no Passover like Yoshiyahu's had been kept since the days of Shemu'el the prophet. His Passover involved properly organized Levitical service, the slaughter of 30,000 Passover lambs and 3,000 bulls, and meticulous attention to the Torah instructions.

faq.question: What was Yoshiyahu's fatal mistake?
faq.answer: He went out to fight Pharaoh Nekho at Megiddo against YHWH's command. Nekho sent messengers saying YHWH had commanded him to hurry and that Yoshiyahu should not interfere — but Yoshiyahu disguised himself and fought anyway, was fatally wounded by archers.

faq.question: What does 2 Divrei HaYamim 36:15-16 say about YHWH's heart toward his people before the destruction?
faq.answer: YHWH had compassion on his people and his dwelling place, and sent his messengers persistently — again and again — to warn them. The people mocked the messengers, despised YHWH's words, and scoffed at his prophets, until there was no remedy.

faq.question: How does the 70-year exile relate to the Shabbat in Divrei HaYamim's theology?
faq.answer: Divrei HaYamim states the land lay desolate to fulfill its Shabbat rest — the land enjoyed its Shabbatot for 70 years. This frames the exile not merely as punishment but as the land receiving the Shabbat years that Yisra'el had not given it.

faq.question: Why do the final verses of Divrei HaYamim repeat the opening of Ezra?
faq.answer: The deliberate link connects the story of YHWH's people directly into the story of restoration. Divrei HaYamim ends on a note of hope — the same words that open Ezra — showing the exile is not the end of the covenant story but a turning point toward restoration.

faq.question: Who was the last king of Yehudah and how did his reign end?
faq.answer: Tzidkiyahu — installed by Nebukhadnetzar — did evil, refused to humble himself before Yirmeyahu, stiffened his neck and hardened his heart, then rebelled against Nebukhadnetzar. Nebukhadnetzar destroyed the Temple, broke down Yerushalayim's walls, and carried the remaining people to Babylon.

faq.question: How does Divrei HaYamim function as a whole theological narrative?
faq.answer: It frames all of Yisra'el's history from Adam to the Cyrus Decree as a single covenant narrative — the Temple as the dwelling place of YHWH's glory, its proper service as the measure of covenant faithfulness, and the exile as the land's Shabbat rest before the return and restoration.
